en: Buddhavamsa 26.
The Lineage of Buddha Kassapa "After Koṇāgamana..."
The Perfectly Enlightened One, supreme among bipeds,
named Kassapa by clan,
was a King of Dhamma and a bringer of light.
Having given to beggars a gift that was abundant in food and drink, yet had been cast away as family refuse, one [reaps the fruit].
Having fulfilled his heart's desire,
like a bull breaking through a fence,
he attained supreme enlightenment.
When Kassapa, the leader of the world, was setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma,
[there were] twenty thousand koṭis...
There was the first clear realization.
When the Buddha wanders on tour through the world for four months,
There was a second realization for ten thousand times ten million [beings],
having performed a twin miracle.
He proclaimed the element of knowledge;
there was a third realization for five thousand times ten million beings.
In the delightful city of the gods, Sudhammā,
he proclaimed the Dhamma there to three thousand koṭis.
The Jina awakened the gods.
In another teaching of the Dhamma, [he did so] for the yakkha Naradeva.
The realizations of these [beings] are incalculable in number.
Of that very God of Gods as well—
There was a single gathering of those whose taints were exhausted, who were stainless,
whose minds were peaceful, and who were steadfast.
At that time, there was a gathering of twenty thousand bhikkhus who had transcended all states of existence.
Possessing modesty and virtue, such was the state of those sages.
At that time, I was a young brahmin known as Jotipāla.
A reciter, a bearer of mantras,
one who has mastered the three Vedas,
and is proficient in the science of marks and traditional lore.
He has reached perfection in the true Dhamma;
he is skilled in both the earth and the sky, a knower of all that should be known, free from all taints.
The Blessed One Kassapa had an attendant named Ghaṭīkāra;
he was respectful and reverential.
Extinguished in the third fruit,
Ghaṭīkāra took me and approached the Conqueror Kassapa.
Having heard his Dhamma,
I went forth in his presence.
Having become one of aroused energy,
Skilled in what is proper and what is improper,
I did not decline in any respect,
and I fulfilled the teaching of the Conqueror.
Having mastered everything spoken by the Buddha, the ninefold teaching of the Victor,
I brought glory to the Conqueror’s dispensation.
Seeing my marvel,
that Buddha also made a prediction:
“In this auspicious aeon,
this one shall become a Buddha.
There was a delightful city called Kapila;”
Having gone forth,
the Tathāgata exerted himself in striving and performed ascetic practices.
Having sat down at the foot of the Ajapāla tree, the Tathāgata there partook of the milk-rice.
He will go to the Nerañjarā.
Having partaken of the milk-rice on the bank of the Nerañjarā, he will proceed.
By the prepared supreme path, he will approach the foot of the Bodhi tree; then,
having performed a circumambulation, he will sit down.
The unsurpassed seat of enlightenment;
in the invincible place,
upon the supreme throne of awakening.
Sitting cross-legged,
he of great renown will awaken.
His mother who gave birth to him—
Her name shall be Māyā;
her father, named Suddhodana,
shall be this Gotama.
Free from taints, devoid of passion,
with peaceful minds and composed,
were Kolita and Upatissa.
The disciples shall be foremost;
one named Ānanda, as his attendant,
shall wait upon this Conqueror.
Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā shall be the foremost female disciples,
free from taints and with peaceful minds.
Free from passion and composed;
the awakening of that Blessed One is called "Assattha."
Cittā and Hatthāḷavakā shall be the foremost attendants;
so too shall be Nandamātā and Uttarā.
"May they be the foremost among those who provide service.
Having heard these words from the great seer of the hermitage,
Men and gods were filled with joy,
exclaiming, "This, they say,
is the seed of a Buddha! Shouts of acclamation arose.
They clap their hands and laugh;
with palms joined in reverence, the ten thousand worlds together with the devas pay homage.
‘If we fail in the teaching of this Lord of the World,
in a future time, [we shall suffer].’
We shall stand face to face with him.
Just as people crossing a river,
having missed a good landing place;
Having taken hold at a ford below,
they cross over the great river; even so, we all—
“If we release this Conqueror,
in a future time we shall stand face-to-face with him.”
Having heard her words as well,
my mind became even more serene;
I resolved upon a further vow.
In order to fulfill the ten perfections.
Thus, having wandered through saṃsāra,
avoiding what is improper;
A difficult task has been accomplished by me for the sake of enlightenment alone.
[In] the city named Bārāṇasī...
You are a kshatriya named Kikī;
you dwell there in that city,
a great family of the Fully Awakened One.
The Buddha’s father was a Brahmin named Brahmadatta;
his mother was named Dhanavatī.
Of Kassapa, the Great Seer.
For two thousand years he dwelt in the household life.
The Haṃsa, Yaśas, and Sirinanda—
these three supreme palaces;
and sixteen thousand.
The women were beautifully adorned;
that woman was named Sunandā,
and her son was named Vijitasena.
Having seen four omens,
he went forth from the palace;
for seven days he practiced ascetic exertion.
The Supreme Person practiced [the path].
Being entreated by Brahmā,
Kassapa, the Leader of the World, [arose].
The Great Hero, the Supreme among Men, set the Wheel in motion at the Deer Park.
Tissa and Bhāradvāja—
They were the chief disciples;
Sabbamitta by name was the attendant of the Great Seer Kassapa.
Anulā and Uruvelā were his chief female disciples;
such was the enlightenment of that Blessed One.
He was called Nigrodha.
Sumaṅgala and Ghaṭīkāra were his chief supporters.
Vicitasena and Bhaddā were his chief attendants. In height, that Buddha—
Reaching twenty ratanas in height,
it was like a lightning-staff in the sky,
or like the moon filled with its constellations.
The lifespan of that Great Seer was twenty thousand years;
remaining for that long, he—
He ferried across a great multitude of people.
Having constructed a pond of Dhamma and provided the ointment of virtue, he gave it away.
Having clothed himself in the Dharma-robe,
having donned the garland of Dharma,
[he beheld] the stainless mirror of Dharma.
Except for the great multitude;
some, aspiring to Nibbāna,
may behold my adornment.
Having donned the armor of virtue,
clad in the mail of meditative absorption,
and having put on the shield of the Dhamma,
Having donned the supreme armor,
and having fastened the shield of mindfulness and the sharp spear of wisdom;
Having given the excellent sword of the Dhamma that crushes attachment to sensual pleasures,
and having bestowed the ornament of the threefold knowledge,
Having given the garland of the four fruits as a head-ornament,
and the jewelry of the six direct knowledges,
together with the flower-garland of the Dhamma.
Having given the white parasol of the True Dhamma, which wards off evil,
and having fashioned the flower of fearlessness,
He has attained Nibbāna along with his disciples.
For he is the Perfectly Enlightened One,
immeasurable and unassailable.
For this is the treasure of the Dhamma,
well-expounded and inviting one to come and see;
for this is the treasure of the Saṅgha.
The unsurpassed one has practiced well;
all that has vanished,
for indeed all conditioned phenomena are empty.
The Conqueror, the Teacher Mahākassapa,
attained Nibbāna in the Setavyā Monastery;
right there stands his Conqueror’s stupa.
“Rising up to the height of a yojana.
This is the twenty-fourth lineage of the Blessed One Kassapa.
